title: Offline-First Reading
reading_goal: Understand the "offline-first" concept, which enables basic learning even without a network connection.
question: What is the purpose of "offline-first"?
choices: To keep the app's core features usable without an internet connection
answer: To keep the app's core features usable without an internet connection
explanation: Offline-first designs locally available core features to work without a network. Calling syncWhenOnline does not prove that the server is reachable, so the app must handle real request failures and retries. Store offline changes in a durable queue, then prevent duplicate application and resolve conflicts after connectivity returns.

title: Read "Local-First"
reading_goal: Understand the "local-first" approach, in which user history is first saved locally and then synchronized later.
question: What are the benefits of "local-first"?
choices: User data can be saved immediately even if the network is slow.
answer: User data can be saved immediately even if the network is slow.
explanation: Local-first applies a change to device storage first for an immediate response, then synchronizes it with the server. Local storage can still fail because of quota limits or browser cleanup, so confirm the write. If multiple devices can edit the same record, use a durable queue, version information, and conflict rules together.

title: Reading the Service Worker Cache
reading_goal: Understand how service workers store app files and data files in the cache to support offline functionality.
question: What is the role of the service worker cache?
choices: Saves app files to the cache so they can be opened quickly again
answer: Saves app files to the cache so they can be opened quickly again
explanation: A service worker's Cache API stores request responses such as the app shell to support offline reopening. cache.addAll can reject the whole operation if one item fails, so handle installation failure. A cache is neither guaranteed permanent storage nor automatically fresh; define version replacement and stale-cache cleanup.

title: Reading the Cache Strategy
reading_goal: Understand how to choose between cache-first and network-first strategies based on the nature of the data.
question: Why are there different cache strategies?
choices: Because freshness and speed requirements differ by resource
answer: Because freshness and speed requirements differ by resource
explanation: Cache-first may suit a rarely changing app shell, while network-first with a timeout and fallback may suit freshness-sensitive data. Choose by update frequency and offline requirements rather than file extension alone. Every strategy still needs behavior for stale data, expiration, and request failure.

title: Reading the sync queue
reading_goal: Understand the sync queue, which stores changes made while offline and sends them when the system comes back online.
question: What is the purpose of the sync queue?
choices: To synchronize changes made while offline with the server later
answer: To synchronize changes made while offline with the server later
explanation: A sync queue holds offline changes for later delivery. The in-memory array in the example can disappear on reload, so a durable store such as IndexedDB may be required. Give each item a stable operation ID and order, remove it only after confirmed success, and retry failures with bounded backoff.

title: Reading "Dirty Record"
reading_goal: Understand what a "dirty record" is—a record that has been modified locally but has not yet been reflected on the server.
question: What does “dirty record” mean?
choices: Data that has been modified locally but has not yet been synchronized
answer: Data that has been modified locally but has not yet been synchronized
explanation: A dirty record was changed locally but has not yet been acknowledged by the server. Persist the flag with the change so a restart does not lose pending work. Clear it only after a successful response, and compare versions so a record edited again during upload is not incorrectly marked clean.

title: Read updated_at
reading_goal: Understand the `updatedAt` timestamp required for determining synchronization conflicts.
question: Why is `updatedAt` important?
choices: To provide useful context about when each copy was modified
answer: To provide useful context about when each copy was modified
explanation: updatedAt is useful metadata, but it cannot by itself prove which change is correct or newer. Device clocks may disagree, and two edits can share a timestamp. Use a server-managed revision or ETag for conflict detection and treat time as supporting information for the user.

title: Read about cloud sync
reading_goal: Understand cloud sync, which allows you to continue the same learning progress across multiple devices.
question: What is the purpose of cloud sync?
choices: To continue your learning progress across multiple devices
answer: To continue your learning progress across multiple devices
explanation: Cloud sync aligns local records from multiple devices with the same server account. One upload is not the whole workflow. Authentication, download, server acknowledgement, deduplication, deletion propagation, and conflict rules are all needed so one device does not silently overwrite another.

title: "Last Write Wins" reading
reading_goal: Understand the "last write wins" strategy, which adopts the most recent revision.
code: winner = max(local, remote, key=lambda x: x.updatedAt)
question: What is the key to "last write wins"?
choices: Selecting the most recently updated data as the final value
answer: Selecting the most recently updated data as the final value
explanation: Last-write-wins chooses the final write according to a defined order. Comparing client updatedAt values can produce the wrong order when device clocks disagree, so a server timestamp or monotonic revision is safer. Any version can still discard earlier content, so important notes need history or user choice.

title: Reading the Merge Strategy
reading_goal: Understand that a merge strategy can be used for data that is easy to combine, such as bookmarks.
question: What kind of data is the merge strategy useful for?
choices: Data that blends together naturally, like a list of bookmarks
answer: Data that blends together naturally, like a list of bookmarks
explanation: A merge strategy combines conflicts according to the data's meaning. Set union is natural when two devices add different bookmarks, but a deletion can reappear unless deletions are represented separately. Free-form notes may be harmed by automatic merging, and progress also needs domain-specific rules rather than simply taking the latest value.

title: Idempotent sync read
reading_goal: Understand idempotent synchronization, which ensures that results remain intact even if the same synchronization request is sent multiple times.
question: Why is idempotent sync necessary?
choices: Because retries may deliver the same request more than once
answer: Because retries may deliver the same request more than once
explanation: Retries can deliver the same request multiple times, so the server should use a stable operationId to recognize work already processed. Upserting an absolute state by ID helps, but it is not sufficient if the operation also increments a score or sends a notification. Duplicate delivery must leave the same state and side effects as one delivery.

answer: To verify that records remain safe through offline use and synchronization
explanation: A sync quality gate tests offline writes, queue recovery after restart, duplicate requests, reconnection, and real conflicts. Checking only field presence is not enough. title: Read the offline sync flow
reading_goal: Understand the entire workflow, from local storage and queue loading to online detection, server synchronization, and conflict resolution.
question: What is the natural sequence of the offline sync flow?
choices: Local storage → Mark as dirty → Add to sync queue → Transfer when online → Resolve conflicts
answer: Local storage → Mark as dirty → Add to sync queue → Transfer when online → Resolve conflicts
explanation: Persist the change locally, then store its dirty flag and stable operation ID in a queue. Do not trust an online signal alone; attempt delivery and confirm server acknowledgement. If versions conflict, resolve them and store the new version, then remove only queue items whose success is confirmed.
